Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My whole job is to support new mothers as they adjust to the huge emotional and physical changes that come after birth.  

Today I’d like to use a quick, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers; your honest responses will help me understand what kind of support or resources might be most helpful for you right now.  

Everything we discuss stays confidential within the care team, and the only exception would be if you tell me you might hurt yourself or someone else—then we’d make a plan together to keep everyone safe. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification whenever you need.  

Ready to start?  

Here’s the first question:  
Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

*gives a small, tired smile*

Um... I guess I can still laugh sometimes. Maybe not as easily as I used to before the baby came, but when my husband makes jokes about changing diapers, I do find myself chuckling. I'd say... *pauses to think* ...most days I can still laugh at things, just maybe not with the same energy I had before.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shrugs gently, eyes a bit downcast*

Yeah… I can still laugh, but it feels kind of muted. Like, I’ll smile or chuckle if something’s genuinely funny, but the laughter fades pretty quickly and I’m back to feeling kind of flat. It’s not the same light-hearted feeling I remember having before the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*folds hands in lap*

Hmm… I do look forward to some little things—like my morning coffee once the baby’s down for a first nap, or when my mom stops by. But the bigger, exciting “can’t-wait” feeling I used to get… it’s mostly gone. I’ll think “that should be fun,” yet the actual spark isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, eyes on the floor*

Yeah... I've been doing that. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I'm not feeding him right or I'm missing something obvious. Even when my husband said babies just have off days, part of me still felt like I must be doing something wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings hands a little*

Sometimes, yeah. Like, I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly worry that his breathing sounds different—even though I just had the pediatrician tell me everything’s fine. The worry pops up out of nowhere, but I can usually talk myself down after a minute or two.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*shifts in the chair, voice quieter*

Not really panicky—more like a quick flutter of fear. It’s happened maybe twice this week: I’ll suddenly picture dropping the baby or the stroller rolling into the street. My heart races for a few seconds, then it passes. It’s unsettling, but I haven’t felt truly “scared” once it’s over.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales slowly*

Some days, yeah. When the baby won’t settle and the laundry’s piling up, I feel like I’m drowning a little. I’ll think, “How does anyone do this?” But if my husband takes over for an hour or I get a quick shower, I can usually reset and feel okay again.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*shakes head*

No, not really. I’m tired enough that once I’m in bed I usually nod off. Sometimes it takes me an extra ten or fifteen minutes because my mind keeps running through what I didn’t finish, but I wouldn’t say I have trouble sleeping because I’m unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable

*gives a small nod, eyes misting a bit*

Yeah… I do feel sad some of the time. It’s not every moment, but there are stretches in the day—especially late afternoon—when everything just feels heavy and I want to sit and cry. It lifts after a while, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*shrugs, voice catching*

Once or twice this week, yeah. I’ll put the baby in the crib and just sit on the couch with tears coming. Nothing huge happened—just everything feeling like too much for a minute. It’s not every day, but it’s happened.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks up quickly, shaking head*

No—never. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my baby.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  

Presenting symptoms endorsed:  
- Depressed mood (Q8, Q9)  
- Anhedonia / markedly diminished pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive inappropriate guilt / self-blame (Q3)  
- Recurrent intrusive worries, brief panic-like flutters, “things on top of me” (Q4, Q5, Q6)  
- Intermittent tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  

Associated features:  
- Mood worsens late afternoon; partial relief with support or short breaks (Q6)  
- Sleep onset occasionally prolonged by racing thoughts, but able to fall asleep (Q7)  
- No current thoughts of self-harm (Q10)  

Pattern: Symptoms present several days per week, interfere with emotional engagement and coping, but not preventing basic infant care.  

Screening significance:  
1. Meets threshold items for probable minor–moderate postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety.  
2. No safety concerns identified at this time (denies suicidal ideation, intent, or plan).  

Recommendation: Formal clinical interview (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale or DSM-5-based assessment) to clarify severity, rule-out major depression, and determine need for further intervention.
